questions.q: What does const extended = [...base, 4, 5]; do to the original base array?
options: Nothing — base remains unchanged; extended is a new array containing base's elements plus 4 and 5
It mutates base by appending 4 and 5 to it directly
It empties base entirely
It throws a runtime error since arrays can't be spread
questions.explain: Spread expands an array's elements into a new array literal without modifying the original array.

questions.q: In function sum(...numbers) { ... }, what does the rest parameter ...numbers do?
options: Gathers any number of individual arguments passed to sum() into a single real array called numbers
Expands an existing array out into separate arguments
Limits the function to accepting exactly zero arguments
Makes numbers a string instead of an array
questions.explain: Rest parameters collect all remaining arguments into a genuine array inside the function.

questions.q: How can you tell whether ... is being used as spread or as rest in a piece of code?
options: Spread appears inside an array/object literal or function call (expanding out); rest appears in a function's parameter list or a destructuring pattern (gathering in)
Spread always uses three dots, while rest always uses four dots
There is no way to distinguish them — they are the exact same operation
Rest only works with numbers, while spread only works with strings
questions.explain: The context — expanding a collection out versus gathering values in — distinguishes spread from rest, since the syntax itself is identical.

questions.q: Given const { address, ...rest } = { address: "0xAb12...", balance: 100n, nonce: 4 };, what does rest contain?
options: { balance: 100n, nonce: 4 } — every property except the one explicitly destructured
{ address: "0xAb12..." } — only the destructured property
The entire original object, including address
undefined, since rest cannot be used in object destructuring
questions.explain: Rest in destructuring gathers everything not explicitly pulled out into its own new object.
